nature-eco-739.title: Seascape ecology: reading patterns in the sea
nature-eco-739.text: A seagrass bed in a sand flat is not just a place; it is a pattern. Seascape ecology studies the causes and ecological consequences of spatial pattern in the marine environment, borrowing the frameworks of landscape ecology. Its central tenet is that patch context matters: surroundings shape local conditions, so the shape, size, arrangement and edges of patches all count. Studies choose scales that fit an organism's movement. Juvenile fish use several habitats as they grow, so ignoring mangrove roots, macroalgae or seagrass can mislead assessments of an estuary. The field has grown since the 1970s, yet in marine systems understanding is still in its infancy.

nature-eco-733.title: Aliso Canyon: the leak that out-damaged Deepwater Horizon
nature-eco-733.text: The worst leak in American history, judged by its environmental effect, was not oil. It was gas. The 2015-2016 Aliso Canyon leak in California released {{ref:nature-eco-727}}, a potent {{ref:nature-eco-162}}. It was described as more damaging to the environment than the Deepwater Horizon leak in the Gulf of Mexico. The comparison shows that an invisible gas escaping into the air can cost the climate more than a spill that blackens a coast.

nature-eco-685.title: Lavakas: the gullies that bleed Madagascar red
nature-eco-685.text: On Madagascar's high plateau, rivers run dark red-brown. The cause is the stripping of vegetation, which has opened gullies called lavakas. Slash-and-burn and shifting cultivation of tropical forests are one cause of high loads of {{ref:nature-eco-682}}, because bare, seared ground is open to wind and water erosion. Some areas have as many as 150 lavakas per square kilometre, and lavakas may account for 84% of all sediments carried off by rivers. Siltation also brings fish kills, along with the costs of managing sediment and siltation.

nature-eco-700.title: Fire suppression: a century of putting out the wrong fires
nature-eco-700.text: For decades the American answer to every wildfire was to put it out. Federal policy in early 20th-century North America aimed to suppress all fires, and it ended the use of {{ref:nature-eco-699}}s. Habitats changed. Oak savannas and canebrakes are now critically endangered, and in the Eastern US fire-sensitive red maple is spreading at the expense of fire-tolerant oaks. Since 1995 the US Forest Service has slowly brought burning back into forest management. The conflict over burning stems from old campaigns against wildfire and the later acceptance of fire as a necessary ecological phenomenon.

nature-val-113.title: Direct damage-cost valuation: counting what pollution breaks
nature-val-113.text: One way to value cleaner air is to add up the damage dirty air does. Direct damage-cost valuation treats an environmental improvement as the reduction in the monetary damage costs of pollution. Types include production damage, such as air pollution lowering corn yields, avoided cost, such as green roofs avoiding storm sewer spending, and health cost measures. The Cabezas text calls these measures deeply problematic. They often give woefully incomplete estimates, since a cancer victim's medical bills are far below what her family would pay to avoid the illness.

nature-val-114.title: The normal distribution and its bell curve
nature-val-114.text:
Most of the statistics behind valuation rest on one shape. The normal distribution is the bell-shaped probability distribution defined by a mean, which sets its location, and a variance, which sets its squared scale. It is symmetric around its mean, which is also its mode and median. About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two and about 99.7% within three: the 68-95-99.7 or 3-sigma rule.

The standard normal is the case with mean 0 and variance 1; any normal variable can be built by scaling it by the standard deviation and shifting it by the mean. Its density is written with the Greek letter phi and its cumulative distribution function with capital Phi. The quantile function of the standard normal is the probit function.

Among all distributions with a given mean and variance, it has the maximum entropy. It is the only one whose cumulants beyond the mean and variance are zero. Any linear combination of independent normal variables is itself normal, and the sum of squares of independent standard normals has a chi-squared distribution. Occurrences are loosely exact, approximate or merely assumed, and Ioannidis warns that using normal standard deviations to validate findings leaves non-normal phenomena untested.

nature-val-115.title: Central limit theorem: why bell curves keep appearing
nature-val-115.text: Add up enough small random effects and a pattern emerges. Under fairly common conditions, the sum of many random variables is approximately normally distributed. The theorem applies to independent, identically distributed variables with the same arbitrary distribution, finite variance and zero mean. As the number of variables grows, the scaled mean approaches a {{ref:nature-val-114}}. This explains why approximately normal distributions turn up in so many situations.

nature-val-107.title: Regulation: rules that steer markets
nature-val-107.text:
Every speed limit and every pollution cap is regulation. It is the management of complex systems according to a set of rules and trends. State-mandated regulation is government intervention in the private market to produce outcomes that would not otherwise occur, from consumer protection to technological advancement. It may prescribe or proscribe conduct (command-and-control), calibrate incentives, or shape preferences. Common examples include limits on environmental pollution, minimum wages, labelling rules and zoning.

A critical question is whether the regulator has enough information to make ex-ante regulation more efficient than ex-post liability for harm, or whether self-regulation is preferable. Modern industrial regulation traces to the UK Railway Regulation Act 1844. In the 1960s and 1970s US concern over regulatory capture led to detailed laws creating the EPA and OSHA.

nature-val-008.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis: the cheapest way to a goal
nature-val-008.text:
Sometimes the goal is fixed and the only question is how to reach it cheaply. Cost-effectiveness analysis compares the costs and outcomes of different courses of action without putting a money value on the outcomes. Unlike {{ref:nature-val-001}}, it does not monetise the effect, which makes it common in health care, where pricing health is seen as inappropriate. Results are usually a ratio of cost to a health gain such as years of life; the most common outcome measure is the quality-adjusted life year. A 1995 review of over 500 life-saving interventions found a median of $42,000 per life-year saved.

It also suits some environmental goals. For a single physical outcome, such as cutting energy use, it can replace cost-benefit analysis and is less laborious. It is preferred in climate economics when the benefits of mitigation and adaptation are hard to express in money. Distributional cost-effectiveness analysis extends it to weigh how outcomes are spread, trading equity against efficiency.

Policy goals are often set politically, such as the Clean Air Act acid rain cut of 10 million tons of sulfur dioxide below 1980 levels, without knowing whether the target is efficient. A policy can still be judged cost-effective. Pollution reduction is split cost-effectively across sources only when all face the same marginal abatement cost. Otherwise, shifting cleanup from a high-cost to a low-cost source cuts total cost.

nature-val-108.title: Deregulation: taking the rules back out
nature-val-108.text: Deregulation is the process of removing or reducing state regulations, typically in the economic sphere. It became common in advanced industrial economies in the 1970s and 1980s. Two ideas drove it: the inefficiency of {{ref:nature-val-107}} and the risk of agencies being controlled by the industries they regulate. Earlier economic regulation was promoted to limit externalities such as pollution and monopolization, but by the late 1970s such reforms were deemed burdensome to growth.

nature-val-109.title: The regulatory state: government by rulebook
nature-val-109.text: Governments can grow without taxing or spending more. The regulatory state is the expansion in the state's use of rulemaking, monitoring and enforcement techniques and institutions. State expansion today is generally via {{ref:nature-val-107}} rather than taxing and spending.

nature-val-110.title: Mild and wild risk: when averages lie
nature-val-110.text: Not all risk behaves alike. Mandelbrot distinguished mild risk, which follows normal or near-normal distributions, from wild risk, which follows fat-tailed distributions. Mild risk obeys the law of large numbers and is relatively predictable. Wild risk, with possibly infinite mean or variance, makes that law ineffective and is hard or impossible to predict. A common error is to assume risk is mild when it is wild. It is a sharper case of {{ref:nature-econ-773}}.

nature-val-111.title: Risk society: dangers we manufacture ourselves
nature-val-111.text: Humans have always faced risks such as natural disasters, usually perceived as caused by non-human forces. Giddens and Beck argued that modern societies face something new: manufactured risks, such as pollution, produced by modernization itself. In their view the danger now comes not only from outside, but from the way societies live. This sharpens the idea of {{ref:nature-econ-773}}.

nature-val-106.title: Pitfalls in cost estimation
nature-val-106.text:
A careless cost estimate can make a good policy look bad, or the reverse. Careful estimates must avoid four common mistakes: ignoring opportunity costs, using the wrong counterfactual, counting non-additional costs and ignoring market changes.

Opportunity costs are not on accounting sheets and are often overlooked. Studies of US endangered-species recovery spending used only direct government costs because opportunity costs are hard to measure. A cursory before-and-after comparison wrongly credits a policy with all cost changes. After the Deepwater Horizon drilling restrictions oil prices rose, but part of the rise came from recovering demand, so the true counterfactual is the price without the restrictions.

Only additional costs count. Temporary stormwater controls already required during construction should not be charged to a new rule requiring no stormwater runoff after building. Additionality is contested in benefit estimation too: some lands paid not to be deforested might not have been, or landowners may be paid by several sources for the same activity.

Markets also move. A methyl bromide ban would raise strawberry production costs, lowering sales. The social cost is the deadweight loss on unsold strawberries plus higher costs on those still sold, which is below the simple estimate that costs all pre-ban output.

nature-val-105.title: Transfers versus real costs
nature-val-105.text: A cost total should count only real changes in behavior or resource use, not transfers of money from one party to another. Take a wetland built for nutrient removal. Its cost is the wetland installation plus the {{ref:nature-econ-095}} of the foregone farming. If a conservation group pays the farmer extra, that is a pure transfer, so the social cost of the wetland does not rise.

nature-val-112.title: Ecological modernization: can markets and states fix the environment?
nature-val-112.text:
Can the economy be greened without being slowed? Ecological modernization is a school of thought arguing that the state and the market can work together to protect the environment. It emerged in the early 1980s among scholars at Free University and the Social Science Research Centre in Berlin, including Joseph Huber, Martin Jänicke and Udo Simonis. Its basic assumption is that economy and ecology can be combined: productive use of natural resources and environmental media can be a source of growth, like labour and capital productivity.

Its tools include energy and resource efficiency, clean technologies, environmental management, substitution of hazardous substances and product design for environment, with radical innovations changing industrial metabolism. It also draws on industrial symbiosis, product life-cycle assessment, and 'cradle to cradle' manufacturing as against 'cradle to grave'. Scholars differ on whether it is only techno-industrial policy or includes cultural change, and on whether government, markets or civil society should lead. All expect innovative structural change.

Business may favour it because it meets the triple bottom line without challenging free-market principles. Many views within the environmental movement see free trade and self-regulation as part of the problem. Critics call it greenwashing that leaves capitalism's impulses to degrade the environment intact. They say it ignores environmental racism, applies mostly to Germany and the Netherlands, and rests on an impossible 'sustainable growth'. Its effectiveness and applicability remain a contentious area of environmental social science.
